title: The Nat as Ontological Unit: Information–Thermodynamic Identity and the Foundations of Physical Theory
content: The natural unit of information (nat), defined via the natural logarithm, occupies a singular position at the intersection of information theory and statistical thermodynamics. This paper argues that the nat is not merely a convenient unit of measurement but constitutes an ontological primitive—the irreducible quantum of physical information through which energy, entropy, and probability are rendered mutually commensurable. We demonstrate that Landauer’s erasure bound achieves its coefficient-free canonical form exclusively in nats (E ≥ kBT per nat), that the Jaynes maximum-entropy derivation of statistical mechanics is naturally formulated in nats, and that the Kullback–Leibler divergence acquires direct thermodynamic meaning when measured in this unit. We further show that the decomposition kB = R/NA reveals the Boltzmann constant as encoding the discreteness of the informational substrate: the smallness of kB is the largeness of Avogadro’s number, and Loschmidt’s 1865 molecular count was, implicitly, the first empirical determination of the number of nat-carrying degrees of freedom per macroscopic volume. We show that spacetime itself, as a dynamical physical structure, is ontologically dependent on the informational ground rather than serving as its container—consistent with the holographic principle, emergent gravity, and entanglement-based approaches to quantum gravity. Building on these results, we advance the thesis that information, quantified in nats and grounded thermodynamically via kB, is the foundational category of physical ontology—prior to, rather than coordinate with or derivative of, energy and spacetime.
